lead: A Bitcoin wallet is a key manager, not a purse. The coins never leave the blockchain; they sit there as unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs) locked to addresses. The wallet holds the private keys that unlock those outputs, builds a transaction from them, signs it, and broadcasts it. Wallets exist because raw keys are unusable by hand: software must track your outputs, choose which ones to spend, compute change, and keep one reliable backup. The same job, done with different storage, runs a phone app for small payments, a hardware device kept in a safe, and an exchange account that holds your balance for you.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for UTXOs and change outputs, and Unit 2 for keys, addresses and signatures.

sections.h3: A wallet manages keys; the coins stay on the chain

blocks.text: A Bitcoin wallet stores private keys, watches the chain for outputs those keys can unlock, builds transactions, and signs them. The coins never enter the wallet. They stay on the ledger as unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs), each locked to an address, as Chapter 4.2 explains. Delete the app and the UTXOs are still there; what you may have lost is the key that unlocks them.
Two questions classify every wallet: is the key online or offline, and is the key yours or a company's?

items: Hot wallet: the key sits on a device connected to the internet, such as a phone app, a desktop program or a browser extension. It pays quickly and is exposed to malware.
Cold wallet: the key is created and kept offline. A hardware wallet signs inside its own chip and sends out only the signature, so the key never reaches the computer.
Custodial wallet: an exchange or payment app holds the keys and shows you a balance. You hold a claim on the operator, not keys.
Non-custodial wallet: you hold the keys, and with them the whole responsibility.

blocks.text: Addresses come in three common forms. P2PKH addresses start with 1 and lock to a hash of a public key. P2SH addresses start with 3 and lock to a script hash, the usual home of multisignature. Native SegWit addresses start with bc1 and use bech32 encoding, which pays lower fees because signature bytes are discounted. All three are public: anyone may pay in, only the key holder may spend out.

sections.h3: One seed phrase, a whole tree of keys

blocks.text: A wallet that stores each private key separately needs one backup per key. A deterministic wallet derives every key from a single starting secret, so one backup restores all of them. In a hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallet those keys form a tree, which is why one device can serve several accounts and thousands of addresses.

items: BIP39 turns fresh randomness into 12 or 24 common English words plus a checksum. This is the seed phrase, also called the recovery phrase. The same words always regenerate the same keys.
PBKDF2 stretches the phrase into a 512-bit seed.
BIP32 hashes that seed with HMAC-SHA512 to give the master private key and a master chain code.
Each child key comes from the parent key, the chain code and an index number, hashed together. The index is the position in the tree.
A hardened step, written with an apostrophe as in 0', mixes in the parent private key, so a leaked parent public key cannot produce hardened children.

blocks.where: m is the master key; 84' is the purpose (BIP84, native SegWit; some wallets write 44' for legacy or 49' for P2SH-SegWit); 0' is the coin type, Bitcoin; the next 0' is the account number; 1 is the change chain, while 0 is the external receiving chain; k is the address index, starting at 0.

blocks.text: Two chains, not one. The external chain hands out a fresh receiving address for each payment; the change chain receives the leftover of each spend. Reusing one address publicly links all its payments, a privacy leak explained in Chapter 4.8. A new address costs nothing to make.

sections.h3: Selecting UTXOs, paying, and keeping the change

blocks.text: A spend starts from the wallet's own UTXO list. The wallet selects inputs that cover the payment plus the fee, sends the payment to the payee, and returns the remainder to itself.

items: List the UTXOs the keys control; their sum is the spendable balance.
Choose a subset worth at least payment + fee. Common rules: largest first for fewest inputs, smallest first to clear dust, or an exact-match search.
Add a change output to a fresh address on the change chain, unless the change is dust, in which case it is dropped and the miner collects it.
Sign every input with the key for its address, then broadcast.

blocks.where: Σ inputs is the total value of the selected UTXOs, payment is the amount sent to the payee, and fee is what the miner may claim; all three in the same unit, BTC or satoshi (1 BTC = 10⁸ satoshi).

blocks.text: Coin control is manual selection: you pick the UTXOs, as you would pick which notes to hand over. It matters for privacy, because merging a KYC-exchange output with a private one links them, and for fees, because many small inputs make a large transaction.

Back up the seed phrase on paper or metal, in two places, never as a photo and never typed into a website. A lost or broken hardware wallet is replaced by restoring the phrase on a new device. A leaked phrase is a total loss: whoever reads it can sign, and a confirmed transaction cannot be reversed.

examples.question: A wallet controls three UTXOs: 0.4 BTC, 0.3 BTC and 0.2 BTC. It must pay 0.6 BTC to a merchant with a fee of 0.0005 BTC. Which UTXOs should it choose, and what change does it create?
steps: Try the pair 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7 BTC. Change = 0.7 − 0.6 − 0.0005 = 0.0995 BTC. Positive, so the pair works.
Check the smaller pair 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 BTC. Change = 0.6 − 0.6 − 0.0005 = −0.0005 BTC. Negative, so it cannot pay the fee and fails.
The pair 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5 BTC is below 0.6 BTC, so it fails at once.
The 0.0995 BTC change goes out as a new output to a fresh address on the change chain.
examples.answer: Spend the 0.4 BTC and 0.3 BTC UTXOs; the transaction pays 0.6 BTC, a fee of 0.0005 BTC, and returns 0.0995 BTC change to the wallet's change chain.
examples.check:
u = [0.4, 0.3, 0.2]
pay, fee = 0.6, 0.0005
chosen = u[0] + u[1]
print(round(chosen, 4))
print(round(chosen - pay - fee, 4))
print(round(u[0] + u[2] - pay - fee, 4))

traps: Saying the wallet file or the app contains the coins. It contains keys; the coins are UTXOs on the chain.
Treating the seed phrase as a password. A password can be reset by an operator; the seed phrase is the key itself and nobody can reset it.
Calling the whole input-output gap a fee. The gap minus the change output is the fee; the change is your own money coming back.
Mixing address prefixes: 1 is P2PKH, 3 is P2SH, bc1 is bech32 SegWit.
Forgetting that an apostrophe in a derivation path means hardened, so m/84'/0'/0'/0/0 differs from m/84/0/0/0/0.

quiz.q: What does a Bitcoin wallet actually store?
quiz.a: Private keys (and the addresses or scripts it watches). The coins stay on the blockchain as UTXOs locked to those addresses.

quiz.q: Name the three common address forms and the leading characters of each.
quiz.a: P2PKH starts with 1, P2SH starts with 3, native SegWit (bech32) starts with bc1.

quiz.q: Why does a deterministic wallet need only one backup for thousands of addresses?
quiz.a: Every key is derived from one seed through the HD tree, so the seed phrase regenerates the whole tree. No per-key backup is needed.

quiz.q: Why does a wallet send change to a new change-chain address each time?
quiz.a: Address reuse links all payments to one address in public. A fresh index on the change chain keeps each spend unlinked and costs nothing.

quiz.q: A wallet holds UTXOs of 0.5, 0.25 and 0.1 BTC. It must pay 0.6 BTC with a fee of 0.0002 BTC. Which UTXOs does it choose and what is the change?
quiz.a: Total needed = 0.6002 BTC. The pair 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75 BTC works: change = 0.75 − 0.6 − 0.0002 = 0.1498 BTC. The pair 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6 BTC gives 0.6 − 0.6002 = −0.0002 BTC, so it fails.
Master key, purpose BIP84 (native SegWit), coin type Bitcoin, account 0, change chain (1), address index 7. It is the eighth change address of the first account.

quiz.q: A student says: 'My phone with a non-custodial hot wallet was stolen, so my Bitcoin is gone.' Analyse when this is true and when it is false.
quiz.a: False if the seed phrase was backed up offline: the thief needs the phone's PIN or unlocked screen to sign, and the owner restores the phrase on a new device. True if there is no backup, or if the phone was unlocked and the wallet had no PIN, since the keys existed only there.

quiz.q: A hardware wallet protects your keys from malware. Why does it not protect you from a website that asks you to type your 24 words?
quiz.a: The device never exposes the key, but the phrase is the key in human-readable form. Typing it hands the whole tree to the site, which can sign anything; the hardware wallet's protection stops at the moment the phrase leaves the device.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real wallets now exchange partially signed transactions (PSBT) so a hardware device and an online node can cooperate without sharing keys, and multisignature setups split one key across three devices. Output script descriptors and Miniscript describe which addresses a wallet should watch, replacing guesswork about derivation paths. Seed backup standards such as SLIP-39 split a phrase into shares. A useful next search is 'BIP32 derivation path' followed by 'PSBT workflow' and 'output script descriptors'.
